chapters.title: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy
chapters.notes:
Book-keeping is the systematic recording of monetary business transactions. Accountancy includes recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and interpreting accounting information. Objectives: maintain records, calculate profit or loss, show financial position, support decisions and provide information to owners, managers, lenders and government. Key terms: capital is the owner's investment; drawings are withdrawals by the owner; assets are resources; liabilities are obligations; debtors owe money to the business; creditors are owed money by the business; revenue is income and expense is a cost. Accounting information is useful but usually records only measurable monetary events and may involve estimates. Example: when the owner invests ₹80,000 cash, cash (asset) and capital both increase.

chapters.title: Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
chapters.notes:
Every transaction has two aspects and equal debit and credit effects. Accounting equation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Traditional rules: Personal—debit the receiver, credit the giver; Real—debit what comes in, credit what goes out; Nominal—debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. Modern view: assets and expenses normally increase by debit; liabilities, capital and income normally increase by credit. Example: rent paid ₹4,000: Rent A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000. Double entry provides a complete record and helps prepare a trial balance, but a trial balance does not reveal every type of error.

chapters.title: Journal
chapters.notes:
The journal is the book of original entry in which transactions are recorded chronologically. A journal entry shows date, accounts and amounts, followed by a narration. Steps: identify accounts, classify them, apply debit-credit rules, record equal amounts and write a short explanation. Examples: started business with cash ₹50,000—Cash A/c Dr. 50,000; To Capital A/c 50,000. Paid rent ₹2,000—Rent A/c Dr. 2,000; To Cash A/c 2,000. Credit purchase of goods from Neha ₹6,000—Purchases A/c Dr. 6,000; To Neha A/c 6,000. Goods for resale are purchases; furniture or machinery bought for use is an asset, not purchases.

chapters.title: Ledger
chapters.notes:
A ledger is the principal book containing separate accounts for assets, liabilities, capital, expenses, incomes and persons. Posting transfers journal information to the relevant ledger accounts. Debit is the left side and credit the right side. To balance an account, total both sides and carry the difference to the smaller side. Debit balances commonly occur in assets and expenses; credit balances commonly occur in liabilities, capital and incomes. Example: cash introduced ₹20,000 and rent paid ₹2,000 gives Cash A/c a debit balance of ₹18,000. Journal is chronological; ledger is classified account-wise.

chapters.title: Subsidiary Books
chapters.notes:
Subsidiary books record similar transactions separately to save time and divide work. Purchases Book records credit purchases of goods for resale only; Sales Book records credit sales of goods; Purchases Returns Book records goods returned to suppliers; Sales Returns Book records goods returned by customers; Cash Book records cash and bank transactions; Bills Receivable and Bills Payable Books record bills; Journal Proper records entries not suited to other books. Cash purchase of goods goes to Cash Book, not Purchases Book. Credit purchase of furniture goes to Journal Proper, not Purchases Book.

chapters.title: Bank Reconciliation Statement
chapters.notes:
A Bank Reconciliation Statement explains the difference between the bank balance in the Cash Book and the Pass Book/bank statement on a particular date. Causes include cheques issued but not presented, cheques deposited but not collected, bank charges, interest, direct deposits, standing instructions, dishonoured cheques and errors. Method: identify the starting balance, understand each item, decide its effect from that starting point, and calculate the adjusted balance. Example with favourable Cash Book balance ₹10,000: add cheques issued but not presented ₹2,000; deduct cheques deposited but not collected ₹1,500 and bank charges ₹200. Pass Book balance = ₹10,300. Add/deduct treatment changes with the starting balance and overdraft situation.

chapters.title: Depreciation
chapters.notes:
Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life. Causes include wear and tear, passage of time and obsolescence. Depreciable amount = cost − residual value. Straight Line Method: annual depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. Example: cost ₹1,00,000, residual value ₹10,000, life 5 years gives ₹18,000 per year. Written Down Value Method: depreciation = opening book value × rate. At 10% on ₹1,00,000, first-year depreciation is ₹10,000 and closing book value ₹90,000. SLM gives an equal annual charge; WDV gives a reducing charge.

chapters.title: Rectification of Errors
chapters.notes:
Rectification means correcting errors in recording, posting, balancing or preparing accounts. Types include omission (transaction not recorded), commission (wrong amount/account/posting), principle (capital and revenue items confused), compensating errors and errors disclosed or not disclosed by a trial balance. A Suspense Account may temporarily hold a trial balance difference until errors are located. Example: furniture ₹5,000 wrongly debited to Purchases A/c: Furniture A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Purchases A/c ₹5,000. To rectify, identify the correct treatment, compare it with the entry made and pass the correcting entry.

chapters.title: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
chapters.notes:
Final accounts determine gross profit, net profit and financial position. Trading Account calculates gross profit: Gross Profit = Net Sales − Cost of Goods Sold. Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Net Purchases + Direct Expenses − Closing Stock. Profit and Loss Account starts with gross profit, adds other incomes and deducts indirect expenses to find net profit. Balance Sheet shows assets, liabilities and capital on a particular date. Adjustments: outstanding expense is added to expense and shown as liability; prepaid expense is deducted and shown as asset; accrued income is added to income and shown as asset; income received in advance is deducted and shown as liability; depreciation is charged to P&L and reduces asset value.

chapters.title: Single Entry System
chapters.notes:
Single Entry System is an incomplete method of recording transactions; it does not record both aspects of every transaction. Personal accounts and cash records may be maintained, but a complete trial balance may not be possible. Under Statement of Affairs method, capital = assets − liabilities. Profit = closing capital + drawings − additional capital − opening capital. Example: opening capital ₹40,000, closing capital ₹55,000, drawings ₹8,000 and additional capital ₹5,000 gives profit ₹18,000. Limitations include incomplete records, difficulty detecting errors and fraud, and less reliable profit figures.

chapters.title: Introduction to Commerce and Business
chapters.notes:
Business is an economic activity involving production, purchase or sale of goods and services, usually to earn profit while satisfying needs. Commerce consists of trade and auxiliaries to trade. Trade is buying and selling; auxiliaries include transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, advertising and communication. Industry includes primary activities (extractive and genetic), secondary activities (manufacturing and construction) and tertiary/service activities. Business objectives include economic goals such as profit, growth and innovation, and social goals such as quality goods, fair prices, employment and environmental responsibility.

chapters.title: Trade
chapters.notes:
Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services. Internal trade occurs within a country and includes wholesale trade (bulk sales to retailers) and retail trade (sales to final consumers). External trade takes place between countries: import means buying from abroad, export means selling abroad and entrepot trade means importing for re-export. Wholesalers provide bulk buying, storage, finance, market information and risk bearing. Retailers provide convenience, product variety, small quantities, customer service and local feedback.

chapters.title: Small Scale Industry and Business
chapters.notes:
Small businesses operate on a comparatively limited scale and are important for employment, entrepreneurship, local resource use, regional development and supply chains. Common challenges include limited finance, technology gaps, marketing difficulties, competition, raw-material issues and managerial constraints. Support may include credit, training, technology assistance, incubation, cluster facilities and market access. MSME investment and turnover classifications can change; consult the latest official government notification rather than relying on old figures.

chapters.title: Forms of Business Organisation – I
chapters.notes:
Sole proprietorship is owned and controlled by one person. Advantages: simple formation, quick decisions, secrecy and direct motivation. Limitations: limited capital, unlimited liability in ordinary proprietorship and dependence on one owner. Partnership is an agreement between persons to share profits of a business carried on by all or any one acting for all. A partnership deed may state capital, profit-sharing ratio, duties, interest, salary and dispute procedures. Partnership offers combined capital and skills but may involve disputes and shared liability.

chapters.title: Forms of Business Organisation – II
chapters.notes:
A co-operative society is a voluntary association formed to promote members' common economic interests through democratic participation and service. Types include consumer, producer, marketing, credit, housing and farming co-operatives. A joint stock company is an incorporated legal entity with capital divided into shares. Features include separate legal existence, perpetual succession and limited liability subject to law. Private and public companies differ in share transfer and public invitation rules; statutory requirements should be checked against current company law.

chapters.notes:

chapters.notes:
Business environment is the combination of internal and external forces affecting business decisions. Internal factors include owners, employees, management, resources and culture. External factors include customers, suppliers, competitors, government, technology, economy, society and nature. PESTLE analysis studies Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors. SWOT identifies Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. Environmental analysis helps identify opportunities, anticipate risks and adapt strategy.

chapters.title: Introduction to Management
chapters.notes:
Management is the process of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling resources to achieve objectives efficiently and effectively. Planning sets objectives and actions; organising allocates tasks and authority; staffing recruits and develops people; directing guides, motivates and communicates; controlling compares actual results with standards and corrects deviations. Top management sets direction, middle management coordinates departments and supervisory management guides daily work. Efficiency means minimising waste; effectiveness means achieving goals.

chapters.notes:
A secretary performs administrative, communication, coordination and record-keeping duties. A company secretary is a specialised professional role supporting governance and statutory compliance. Important qualities include integrity, confidentiality, accuracy, punctuality, communication, organisation, tact and legal awareness. Duties may include correspondence, records, meeting arrangements, document preparation and coordination. Company secretarial responsibilities are governed by applicable company law.

chapters.title: Joint Stock Company
chapters.notes:
A joint stock company is an incorporated association with a separate legal identity, capital divided into shares and continuity independent of changes in membership. Features include separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability subject to law and regulated management. Advantages include ability to raise capital, continuity and professional management. Limitations include legal formalities, disclosure requirements and possible delays in decisions.

chapters.notes:
Company formation commonly involves promotion and incorporation, followed by commencement requirements where applicable. Promoters identify the business opportunity, assess feasibility, arrange resources and prepare documents. Incorporation application is filed with the Registrar of Companies using prescribed documents and declarations. The Certificate of Incorporation establishes the company's legal existence. Current forms, fees and filing procedures must be checked on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal.

chapters.notes:

Articles of Association (AOA) contain internal management rules, such as share procedures, meetings and director matters. A prospectus is a disclosure document used when securities are offered to the public, where applicable. MOA defines the framework; AOA regulates internal management, both subject to law.

A shareholder holds shares; the terms often overlap but are not identical in every legal situation. Membership may arise through subscription, allotment, transfer, transmission or other lawful means. Rights may include voting, receiving notices and declared dividends, and inspecting permitted records. Duties include paying amounts due and complying with the company's constitution.

Common types include Annual General Meetings, Extraordinary General Meetings, class meetings and board meetings. Notice informs participants; agenda lists business; quorum is the minimum attendance; a resolution is a formal decision; minutes are the official record. Participants include investors, depositories, DPs, issuers and registrars/transfer agents. Benefits include reduced paperwork, lower risk of loss or forgery, faster transfer and easier portfolio management. Use authorised intermediaries and protect account credentials.

chapters.title: Basic Concepts in Economics
chapters.notes:
Economics studies how individuals and society use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. Scarcity requires choice and creates opportunity cost—the next best alternative sacrificed. Microeconomics studies individual consumers, firms and markets; macroeconomics studies aggregates such as national income, inflation and unemployment. Positive statements describe what is; normative statements express what ought to be. Economic activities include production, consumption, exchange and distribution.

chapters.title: Utility Analysis
chapters.notes:
Utility is the want-satisfying power of a good or service. Total utility is satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the additional satisfaction from one more unit. The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, other things equal, marginal utility tends to decline as more units of a good are consumed in a period. Utility is subjective and depends on preferences, time and circumstances. Example: the first glass of water when thirsty may provide more additional satisfaction than a later glass.

chapters.title: Demand Analysis
chapters.notes:
Demand means the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices during a period. The law of demand states that, other things equal, quantity demanded generally rises when price falls and falls when price rises. A demand schedule lists price and quantity; a demand curve usually slopes downward. Determinants include income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations and number of buyers. A change in own price causes movement along the curve; other factors shift the curve.

chapters.title: Elasticity of Demand
chapters.notes:
Price elasticity of demand measures responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. Percentage method: Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price (often expressed in absolute value). Demand may be elastic, inelastic, unitary, perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic. Influences include availability of substitutes, necessity, proportion of income spent and time to adjust. Elasticity helps firms and governments understand the effect of price changes.

chapters.title: Supply Analysis
chapters.notes:
Supply is the quantity producers are willing and able to offer for sale at different prices during a period. The law of supply states that, other things equal, quantity supplied generally rises with price. A supply curve usually slopes upward. Determinants include input costs, technology, taxes, subsidies, number of sellers, expectations and natural conditions. Own-price changes cause movement along the curve; other factors shift supply.

chapters.title: Market
chapters.notes:
A market is an arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods or services. Market structures include perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly. They differ in number of firms, product differentiation, entry barriers and control over price. Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers with homogeneous products and relatively free entry; monopoly has a single seller with strong barriers. Real markets may combine features.

chapters.title: Index Numbers
chapters.notes:
An index number measures relative change in a variable or group of variables over time, usually with a base period set to 100. Price indices measure price-level changes; quantity indices measure quantities; value indices measure total value. A simple price relative = (current price ÷ base price) × 100. Weighted indices give different importance to items. Uses include studying inflation, cost of living and economic trends. Limitations include choice of base year, items, weights and data quality.

chapters.title: National Income
chapters.notes:
National income accounting measures the value of economic production and income over a period. GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country's domestic territory in a period. GNP/GNI adjusts for net factor income from abroad depending on the measure. Methods include product/value-added, income and expenditure methods. Avoid double counting by counting final output or value added. National income helps compare economic performance but does not alone measure equality, unpaid work or quality of life.

Direct taxes are imposed directly on income or wealth; indirect taxes are imposed on goods and services and may be passed to consumers. Public expenditure supports infrastructure, education, health, security and welfare. A budget presents estimated receipts and expenditure for a period. Fiscal policy uses taxation and spending to influence economic activity.

A central bank issues currency (subject to the monetary system), acts as banker to government and banks, manages reserves and conducts monetary policy. Software includes system software (operating systems and utilities) and application software. The CPU contains the control unit and arithmetic logic unit. RAM is volatile working memory; ROM is non-volatile. Storage devices retain data. Data becomes useful information when processed in context.

chapters.title: Spreadsheet Applications
chapters.notes:

Biotic components include producers, consumers and decomposers; abiotic components include air, water, soil, light and temperature. Food chains show energy transfer; food webs connect multiple chains. Energy flows through trophic levels while nutrients are recycled. Ecosystem balance can be affected by pollution, habitat loss and invasive species.

Prevention is better than treatment: reduce unnecessary consumption, reuse products, segregate waste, recycle suitable materials and dispose of hazardous waste through authorised systems. chapters.title: Development of Physical Fitness
chapters.notes:
Meaning: Physical fitness is the ability to perform everyday activities efficiently, without undue fatigue, while retaining energy for recreation and unexpected demands.

Main components:
• Health-related fitness: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
• Skill-related fitness: speed, agility, balance, coordination, power and reaction time.

Importance: Regular physical activity supports heart and lung function, stronger muscles and bones, mobility, concentration, sleep and general wellbeing.

Ways to develop fitness: walking, running, cycling, swimming, games, mobility exercises and age-appropriate strength activities. Increase activity gradually, warm up, cool down, drink water and allow recovery.

Training principles: regularity, progression, overload in a safe and suitable amount, specificity, variety and recovery.

Revision points: Fitness is multidimensional; one test cannot measure every component. Activities should suit the person's age, ability and health.

chapters.title: Obesity
chapters.notes:
Meaning: Obesity is a medical condition involving excess body fat that may affect health. It is influenced by several factors and should be discussed without stigma.

Contributing factors may include genetics, environment, sleep, stress, medicines, health conditions, food availability and patterns of physical activity.

Possible health effects: increased risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, some heart conditions, joint problems and sleep-related difficulties. Effects vary from person to person.

Assessment: Health professionals may use growth charts, BMI-for-age and other clinical information. Adult BMI cut-offs should not be applied to children and teenagers without professional interpretation.

Prevention and support: regular enjoyable activity, balanced meals, adequate sleep, supportive family and school environments, and advice from qualified health professionals. Avoid crash diets, shame and body comparisons.

Key idea: Focus on health, habits and wellbeing rather than appearance or a number on the weighing scale.

chapters.title: Nature and Diet
chapters.notes:
Meaning of diet: Diet is the food and drink a person regularly consumes. A balanced diet supplies energy and nutrients needed for growth, repair and normal body functions.

Major nutrients:
• Carbohydrates: an important energy source.
• Proteins: support growth and repair of body tissues.
• Fats: provide energy, help absorb certain vitamins and support normal body functions.
• Vitamins and minerals: help regulate body processes and maintain health.
• Water: supports temperature regulation, digestion and transport of substances.
• Fibre: supports healthy digestion.

Balanced food choices: include a variety of cereals or millets, pulses, vegetables, fruits, dairy or suitable alternatives, nuts and seeds. Needs differ by age, activity and health.

Nature and food: local seasons, climate, agriculture and availability influence food habits. Traditional food knowledge can be considered alongside nutrition science.

Remember: No single food provides every nutrient. Avoid extreme restrictions and follow qualified advice for special dietary needs.

chapters.title: Yoga and Mudra
chapters.notes:
Yoga: A traditional discipline that combines physical postures (asanas), breathing practices, concentration and relaxation. Its broader aim includes coordination of body and mind.

Common elements:
• Asana: a posture practised with awareness and stability.
• Pranayama: regulated breathing practices.
• Meditation: training attention and awareness.
• Relaxation: practices that help calm the body and mind.

Mudra: A symbolic or prescribed gesture, often involving the hands, used in some yoga and meditation traditions.

Potential benefits: improved body awareness, flexibility, balance, relaxation and concentration when practised appropriately.

Safety: learn from a qualified instructor, practise in a suitable space, do not force a posture or hold the breath uncomfortably, and stop if pain or dizziness occurs. People with health concerns should seek professional guidance.

chapters.title: Doping (Stimulants)
chapters.notes:
Meaning: Doping refers to the use of prohibited substances or methods to gain an unfair advantage in sport or to enhance performance in ways banned by anti-doping rules.

Why it is prohibited: it undermines fair competition, can endanger health and damages trust in sport.

Stimulants: substances that affect the central nervous system. Some are prohibited in sport because they may create unfair advantages and carry health risks.

Possible risks of misuse: disturbed sleep, anxiety, raised heart rate or blood pressure, dehydration and other serious effects. Risks depend on the substance and the person.

Anti-doping principles: athletes are responsible for checking applicable rules, using medicines only with appropriate medical advice, and following official therapeutic-use procedures where relevant.

Values: fair play, honesty, respect, health and sportsmanship. Never experiment with performance-enhancing substances.

chapters.title: Injury Management
chapters.notes:
Sports injury: Damage or pain affecting muscles, bones, joints, ligaments or tendons during physical activity.

Broad categories:
• Acute injuries: occur suddenly during an activity.
• Overuse injuries: develop gradually through repeated stress without enough recovery.

Prevention: warm up, learn correct technique, use suitable equipment and footwear, follow rules, maintain safe playing conditions, hydrate and allow rest.

Immediate response: stop the activity, protect the injured area and tell a responsible adult, coach or teacher. Do not continue playing through significant pain.

First aid: provide only care within your training and seek qualified medical help when needed. Urgent assessment is important for severe pain, suspected fracture, head or neck injury, breathing difficulty, fainting or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Return to sport: resume only when appropriately assessed and recovered, following guidance from a healthcare professional.

chapters.title: Modern Technology - Activism
chapters.notes:
Meaning: Modern technology can encourage physical activity and support sport, fitness education and performance analysis.

Examples:
• Pedometers and activity trackers record steps and movement.
• Heart-rate monitors provide information about exercise intensity.
• GPS devices help analyse movement in some sports.
• Video analysis helps coaches and players review technique.
• Online platforms provide demonstrations and learning resources.

Benefits: feedback, goal tracking, access to instruction, performance analysis and wider participation.

Limitations: devices may not be perfectly accurate; data privacy, screen time, cost and over-reliance are concerns.

Responsible use: treat device readings as estimates, protect personal data, balance screen use with actual movement and follow qualified coaching advice.

chapters.title: Career Opportunities in Sports
chapters.notes:
Sports offers careers both on and off the playing field.

Examples:
• Athlete or professional player.
• Physical education teacher.
• Coach or assistant coach.
• Fitness trainer, after appropriate recognised training.
• Sports administrator or event organiser.
• Sports journalist, commentator or content professional.
• Referee or umpire, after sport-specific certification.
• Sports physiotherapy and sports medicine, which require relevant professional qualifications.
• Sports photography, equipment management and facility operations.

Useful qualities: discipline, communication, teamwork, leadership, subject knowledge, ethical conduct and continuous learning.

Career planning: identify interests, research recognised courses and qualifications, gain supervised experience and check eligibility requirements for each role.

chapters.title: Various Games
chapters.notes:
Games develop physical skills, cooperation, discipline and sportsmanship. The textbook introduces different games and their basic rules, equipment and playing areas.

When studying each game, prepare:
1. Name and objective of the game.
2. Number of players and team roles, as prescribed.
3. Playing area and important measurements.
4. Equipment required.
5. Basic rules and method of scoring.
6. Fundamental skills and common fouls.
7. Officials and their responsibilities.
8. Safety precautions and sportsmanship.

Examples of team games commonly studied in school physical education include volleyball, football, basketball, cricket and hockey. Use the prescribed textbook for the exact games and official measurements.

Revision tip: make a comparison table for each game using the headings above.

chapters.title: Various Sports Competitions
chapters.notes:
Meaning: A sports competition is an organised event in which individuals or teams take part according to established rules to determine results or rankings.

Common formats:
• Knockout: a participant or team is eliminated after a loss, according to the draw.
• League: participants play a series of matches; points determine standings.
• Combination: uses more than one format, such as league stages followed by knockout rounds.

Organisation includes registration, eligibility, fixtures, venues, officials, equipment, first aid, schedules, scoring and result records.

Values: fair play, respect for officials and opponents, teamwork, discipline and acceptance of results.

For examinations, learn the formats, their features, advantages and limitations as explained in the prescribed textbook.
